summary: Analyzes threats against the Geopriv protocol architecture, including protocol threats, threats from entities storing data, and the abuse of information Geopriv yields. It lists security properties that answer those threats as a reference for requirements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a safe for secrets, you think about who might try to break in and how. This lists those possible troublemakers for location-sharing systems and what protections are needed.

questions: what are the threats to location privacy
subtitle: A catalogue of the ways location information can be stolen, faked, flooded or misused, and the protections that follow.

tldr.problem: Location-based services let people locate themselves and others, and records of those exchanges can reveal habits, whereabouts and associations. The Geopriv design has to work with any device, any relationship between the parties and any legal framework, which makes protecting that data hard.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through attacker motivations and three families of attack (on the protocol, on hosts that store data, and through abuse of the information), then derives the security properties that would counter them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational reference for the Geopriv requirements. It lists needed properties such as authentication, confidentiality, replay protection and default rules, but it specifies no protocol itself.

today: RFC 3694 is an Informational document that was updated by RFC 6280. It describes threats and desirable properties and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why Location Data Needs a Threat Analysis
sections.content:
RFC 3694 analyzes threats against the Geopriv protocol architecture. Location-based services let users find their own location and the location of others, and records of location exchanges can reveal significant information about the habits, whereabouts and associations of individual users.

Geopriv has to support a wide variety of uses of Location Information (LI), many classes of Viewers and any technology, Target-Viewer relationship or legal framework. The RFC says that this breadth complicates protecting privacy and security. It also admits that some threats, such as failure to meet contractual obligations, may fall outside the Geopriv charter, but argues that discussing them is still needed to find desirable security properties.

The RFC notes that risk varies: a server selling location information to marketers is a distinctly lower risk than an outsider intercepting a Target's present location to commit a physical attack.
sections.plainLanguage: If a map app knows where you are, someone could use that to follow you. So the authors first list everything that could go wrong, from nosy neighbors to people who want to cause harm.

sections.title: The Setting and the Attackers
sections.content:
Geopriv is expected to run on the open Internet, where attackers can inspect packets on the wire, spoof Internet addresses and launch large-scale denial-of-service attacks. The main roles are the Location Generator (the source of location information), the Location Server (which may groom or filter the data), the Location Recipient and the Rule Holder who passes Rules to the server. That gives several points where data crosses the wire and needs protection. The RFC also warns that Generators and Recipients may be low-cost devices for which strong cryptography is currently prohibitively expensive computationally.

Attackers may want to learn a private location, or learn it more precisely than the Rule Maker allows. Others want to block, corrupt or redirect location information, find a Target's associates or routines, identify everyone in a place, or halt a whole Geopriv system. A separate class are authorized participants who abuse the data, for example by distributing or accumulating it outside their agreements for commercial gain or unlawful surveillance.
sections.plainLanguage: Some troublemakers want to know where you are, some want to send people the wrong place, and some just want to break the whole system. Even a friend you trusted could misuse what they learn.

sections.title: Attacks on the Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates protocol attacks with invented scenarios. In a hide-and-seek game, a cheating seeker might eavesdrop on the Generator-to-Server or Server-to-referee connection, or impersonate the referee, the Location Server or the Rule Maker. The needed properties are confidentiality on both connections and authentication and authorization of Recipients, Servers and Rule Makers.

Identity spoofing is shown by a rival who wants to fake a coworker's trip, by spoofing Generator traffic or replaying a genuine old location object. This calls for the Server to authenticate Generators, Recipients to authenticate Servers, and protection against replay. Spoofing a Viewer's identity also matters because that identity often decides what is revealed.

Information gathering means traffic analysis: from the fact of transmissions alone, an eavesdropper can learn who interacts with whom, and over time learn associates and routes. The RFC says such threats are difficult to meet with protocol security measures but important to note.

Denial of service would likely target the Location Server, a natural single point of failure. It can act as an exploder, delivering rapid updates to many Seekers, and the cost of checking credentials means floods of spoofed messages could hurt more than generic packet flooding. The RFC calls for stateless authentication challenges and Rule-based limits on the rate at which LI is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone can listen in on your messages, pretend to be someone else, notice who talks to whom, or flood the mail room so nothing gets through. Each trick needs its own kind of lock.

sections.title: Attacks Through Stored Data and Rules
sections.content:
Data stored at servers can be released by accident, sold intentionally despite the Rule Maker's Rule, misused by an employee, stolen by an outside hacker, or subpoenaed without notice to the Target. Stored data can also support traffic analysis, letting someone assemble a history of where a Target has been, for how long, and with whom.

Devices that keep logs pose similar risks and can be the subject of a subpoena or warrant. A screen can be seen by others, spoken directions can be overheard, and a lost or stolen device may expose who received LI and when. Data kept by the Viewer raises the same kinds of risk.

Even the Rules can leak. A Rule that degrades all information by approximately 25 miles tells an interceptor how to recover the true location. The RFC's example of telling a boss an employee is in the building when they are not shows how a Rule can reveal the relationship and that the employee is hiding something.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a locked diary can cause trouble if it is lost, read over your shoulder or demanded by a court. And the rules you write about who may know things can themselves give away secrets.

sections.title: Overcollection and Fair Information Practices
sections.content:
Weak or absent default privacy rules leave location information exposed. Many users lack the skill or motivation to write rules, and without defaults a device might signal to anyone nearby at regular intervals or answer anyone who queries it. A missing "Do not re-distribute" default lets a Location Server pass a Target's location on, and a missing retention limit raises the risk to stored data. The RFC says that defining default rules is beyond its scope, but that they are necessary.

As countermeasures, the RFC lists seven fair information practices that should be reflected in technical systems and Rules: Openness, Individual Participation, Collection Limitation, Data Quality, Finality, Security and Accountability. For example, Finality means data should be used only for the purposes specified when it was collected, so a business given LI to provide directions should use it only for that.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody sets any rules, a phone might tell everyone nearby where it is. Good habits for handling private information, like only collecting what you need and only using it for what you said, help prevent that.

sections.title: Security Properties Geopriv Should Have
sections.content:
The RFC closes by listing properties that answer the threats. It notes some overlap with the requirements in RFC 3693.

  • Rules: the Rule Maker should define Rules, Geopriv should have default Rules that at minimum limit disclosure and retention, a Viewer should learn only the Rules it must obey, and certain Rules, such as when to purge data, should travel with the Location Object.
  • Identity protection: short-lived identifiers for the Target and unlinked pseudonyms for the Location Recipient let a server authenticate a transmission without learning true identities.
  • Transmission security: Rules may limit request frequency (the example is one request honored every 2 hours for city-level data), and the protocol needs mutual end-point authentication, integrity and confidentiality, and replay protection.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence saying the document characterizes potential threats, and the IANA section says it introduces no considerations for IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a set of good locks: only share what the owner allows, use throwaway nicknames instead of real names, make sure both sides prove who they are, and never accept an old message as if it were new.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN FAIR INFORMATION PRACTICES (RFC 3694, SECTION 5.1)

items.title: Openness
items.text: The existence and purpose of a record-keeping system must be known.

items.title: Individual Participation
items.text: People can view, correct or remove data about them.

items.title: Collection Limitation
items.text: Collect lawfully and fairly, and only what the transaction needs.

items.title: Data Quality
items.text: Data is relevant, accurate, complete and timely.

items.title: Finality
items.text: Use and disclose data only for the purposes stated at collection.

items.title: Security
items.text: Reasonable safeguards against loss, unauthorized access and misuse.

items.title: Accountability
items.text: Record keepers answer for complying with these practices.

references.text: Cuellar, J., Morris, J., Mulligan, D., Peterson, J. and J. Polk, "Geopriv Requirements", RFC 3693, January 2004.
